fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Dylan's Phoenician Reading of Norse Gods", "body": "Dylan argues that the Norse pantheon carries Phoenician names in disguise. He reads Tyre, written Sur in Phoenician and glossed as rock or lord, through the Tiwaz rune to Tyr, the war god behind Tuesday, and through the swap of theta and T to Thor. He says Punic becomes Runic once the Greek letter for R is recognised, ties the Aesir to Caesar and his own family name, and hears Odin's epithet Herjan as lord of the host. The Prose Edda's description of Odin as a god of cargos is raised as a nod to seaborne trade."}, {"title": "Alphabets as Trade Tools, Not Languages", "body": "Dylan opens with Higgins and Davies on the sixteen letters said to be shared by Cadmus, the old Latins, Germans, Irish and British bards, then tests Chance by writing Puni in Etruscan, Phoenician and Hebrew letters. His point, set beside Chinese script read aloud differently across many dialects, is that Phoenician may have been an alphabet and mercantile trade script rather than a spoken tongue, just as runes are an alphabet over a Germanic language. Chance shows how the aspirated H slides toward C and K with hoarse and coarse, and Dylan cites the Marsiliana tablet as an Etruscan abecedarium he says is older than any Greek alphabet."}, {"title": "Tracing the Holy Sailors' Guild", "body": "The title of Dylan's book The Holy Sailors comes from the Pelasgi, whom he identifies with the Phoenicians, and he quotes Bishop Thirlwall calling the Cyclopean walls of Tiryns and Mycenae Pelasgian work, adding the Americas himself. He pictures a guild of priests for astronomy and letters, navigators, masons and merchants with ports, marts and mines, and sets out a method: a word match could be coincidence, so look for shared architecture, metallurgy, tools, art and rites until the dots pile up. Mexico's Coxcox flood story, set against its lack of iron smelting when the Spaniards arrived, is the kind of puzzle he says the model must answer."}, {"title": "Questioning Greek-First and Eastern-First History", "body": "Dylan argues that scholars remain under the spell of Mosaic history, which needs civilisation to flow from East to West. He cites Aylett Sammes on the Greeks renaming Phoenician places and myths, Lemprière on the rude early Graeci, and Betham on Etruscan and Phoenician gods being the same, saying the Greeks drew Athena from Tinia while the Latins took Minerva from the Etruscans. He also claims Latin does not descend from Greek, calls Sanskrit a preserved priestly language, and argues that Buddhist astrology naming Mercury as Buddha must postdate the first century AD, which points him toward Alexandria."}, {"title": "Britain, the North and the Trade Empire", "body": "Following Sammes, Dylan says Britain's name came from the Phoenicians, who knew it among the Cassiterides or Tin Islands, and he doubts the island lay idle before Julius Caesar, arguing Caesar came to secure tribute from British kings and describing the druid Diviciacus as Caesar's friend. He traces the so-called Norse to Britain, noting that even mainstream dates for the raids begin there in 793, and mentions Irish monks speaking Latin in Iceland before the Vikings. Trade is treated as quiet conquest, with Webster's 1828 defining purchase as to conquer, and Dylan stays skeptical of the newly reported Vindelev gold hoard until more is known about its gold."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dylan Saccoccio returns to InnerVerse for an Inner Whirled livestream on what he argues are the Phoenician roots of Norse mythology. Chance and Dylan follow the Punic root to Runic, Tyre to Tyr and Thor, and what Dylan calls the holy sailors through alphabets, Cyclopean masonry, Britain and Scandinavia. Along the way they question Greek-first and Eastern-first accounts of history and weigh claims of diffusion reaching China, Mexico and Japan.
